purpose: Deep structured layer connecting trajectory, state spaces, topology, symmetry, gauge theory, Standard Model structure and quantum spin, while explicitly separating physical theory from comparative project interpretation.
epistemic_rule: physics-mathematics is not evidence for supernatural beings; symbolic parallels are tagged separately

nodes.name: Trajectory
nodes.definition: An ordered history through a state space; in classical mechanics a solution curve in phase space, while in quantum theory transition amplitudes require a richer treatment than one classical microscopic path.

nodes.name: State Space
nodes.definition: Space whose points encode possible states of a system; its coordinates depend on the theory and can include positions, momenta, fields, internal degrees of freedom or quantum states.

nodes.name: Configuration Space
nodes.definition: Space of configurations of a system after imposing the relevant constraints; for many-particle systems it is not simply ordinary physical space.

nodes.name: Phase Space
nodes.definition: Space of generalized positions and conjugate momenta; Hamiltonian trajectories are curves generated by the Hamiltonian flow.

nodes.name: State Transition
nodes.definition: Change from one allowed state or configuration to another under dynamical evolution, measurement, interaction or effective description.

nodes.name: Path Integral
nodes.definition: Feynman formulation in which amplitudes are assembled from contributions associated with histories between boundary conditions; it is not equivalent to claiming a particle literally traverses every classical path.

nodes.name: Action Functional
nodes.definition: Functional assigning an action to a history; stationary-action structure underlies classical equations and enters quantum path-integral amplitudes.

nodes.name: Configuration-Space Topology
nodes.definition: Topological structure of the space of allowed configurations; nontrivial loops can affect quantum exchange and phase behavior.

nodes.name: Fundamental Group
nodes.definition: Group of homotopy classes of loops based at a point; it detects global connectivity information invisible to local coordinates.

nodes.name: Homotopy
nodes.definition: Continuous deformation between maps or paths; homotopy classes identify structures equivalent under allowed continuous deformation.

nodes.name: Homology
nodes.definition: Algebraic machinery assigning groups that detect cycles, boundaries and holes in spaces.

nodes.name: Cohomology
nodes.definition: Dual algebraic framework detecting global structure and supporting characteristic classes and geometric phase constructions.

nodes.name: Fiber Bundle
nodes.definition: Space locally resembling a product of base and fiber while allowing nontrivial global gluing; central to geometric descriptions of gauge fields.

nodes.name: Principal Bundle
nodes.definition: Bundle carrying a free action of a structure group; gauge potentials can be represented as connections on principal bundles.

nodes.name: Connection
nodes.definition: Geometric rule for comparing fibers along directions; in gauge theory it represents the gauge potential and defines parallel transport.

nodes.name: Curvature
nodes.definition: Failure of parallel transport around infinitesimal loops to return trivially; represented by field strength in gauge theory.

nodes.name: Holonomy
nodes.definition: Transformation obtained by parallel transport around a closed loop; records global information about a connection.

nodes.name: Gauge Field
nodes.definition: Field associated with local gauge redundancy; its connection and curvature encode interactions in gauge theories.

nodes.name: Gauge Symmetry
nodes.definition: Local redundancy in the description of gauge fields; physical formulations require constraints and gauge-invariant observables rather than treating every gauge-related configuration as a distinct physical state.

nodes.name: Lie Group
nodes.definition: Continuous group with smooth manifold structure, providing the mathematical language for continuous symmetries and gauge groups.

nodes.name: Lie Algebra
nodes.definition: Infinitesimal algebraic structure associated with a Lie group; generators and commutators organize continuous symmetries.

nodes.name: Representation
nodes.definition: Realization of an abstract group or algebra as transformations on a vector space; particle species are classified by representations of spacetime and internal symmetries.

nodes.name: Poincare Group
nodes.definition: Spacetime symmetry group generated by translations and Lorentz transformations; its unitary representations classify relativistic one-particle states.

nodes.name: Lorentz Group
nodes.definition: Symmetry group preserving the Minkowski metric; its representations organize relativistic spin and transformation properties.

nodes.name: Spin Group
nodes.definition: Double cover of the special orthogonal group; Spin groups allow spinor representations unavailable as ordinary tensor representations of SO(n).

nodes.name: Spin Structure
nodes.definition: Additional global structure on a manifold enabling globally defined spinor fields when the relevant obstruction vanishes.

nodes.name: Spin
nodes.definition: Intrinsic angular momentum represented through irreducible representations of spacetime symmetry; it is not literally a tiny classical object rotating around an axis.

nodes.name: Angular Momentum
nodes.definition: Generator of rotations; total angular momentum combines orbital and intrinsic contributions where appropriate.

nodes.name: Spin 1/2
nodes.definition: Half-integer spin representation characteristic of Standard Model fermions; requires spinor representations and exhibits fermionic statistics in local relativistic QFT.

nodes.name: Spin 1
nodes.definition: Integer-spin representation characteristic of Standard Model gauge bosons such as photon, gluons and W/Z bosons.

nodes.name: Spin 0
nodes.definition: Scalar representation; the Standard Model Higgs boson has zero intrinsic angular momentum.

nodes.name: Helicity
nodes.definition: Projection of spin along the direction of momentum; for massless particles it is Lorentz-invariant under proper orthochronous transformations.

nodes.name: Chirality
nodes.definition: Eigenvalue structure of gamma-five for spinor fields; distinct from helicity for massive particles and central to chiral gauge interactions.

nodes.name: Weyl Spinor
nodes.definition: Irreducible chiral spinor representation in four-dimensional relativistic theory.

nodes.name: Dirac Spinor
nodes.definition: Four-component spinor representation combining left- and right-handed Weyl components in four-dimensional relativistic field theory.

nodes.name: Clifford Algebra
nodes.definition: Algebra generated by a vector space with a quadratic form; provides the algebraic framework behind gamma matrices and spinors.

nodes.name: Spin-Statistics Connection
nodes.definition: Under the assumptions of relativistic local quantum field theory, integer-spin fields have bosonic statistics and half-integer-spin fields have fermionic statistics.

nodes.name: Fermion
nodes.definition: Matter-particle class with half-integer spin; quarks and leptons are fermions in the Standard Model.

nodes.name: Boson
nodes.definition: Particle class with integer spin; Standard Model force carriers and the Higgs are bosonic.

nodes.name: Standard Model
nodes.definition: Quantum field theory describing electromagnetic, weak and strong interactions through the gauge structure SU(3) x SU(2) x U(1), with quarks, leptons, gauge bosons and the Higgs sector.

nodes.name: Standard Model Gauge Group
nodes.definition: SU(3)_C x SU(2)_L x U(1)_Y gauge structure, with color, weak-isospin and hypercharge factors before electroweak symmetry breaking.

nodes.name: SU(3) Color
nodes.definition: Non-Abelian color gauge symmetry underlying quantum chromodynamics; quarks transform in the fundamental representation and gluons in the adjoint.

nodes.name: SU(2) Weak
nodes.definition: Non-Abelian weak-isospin gauge factor acting chirally on left-handed fermion doublets.

nodes.name: U(1) Hypercharge
nodes.definition: Abelian gauge factor whose combination with weak isospin produces electromagnetism after electroweak symmetry breaking.

nodes.name: Electroweak Symmetry Breaking
nodes.definition: Higgs-field vacuum structure breaks SU(2)_L x U(1)_Y to U(1)_em while leaving the photon massless and generating masses for W/Z and fermions through Yukawa couplings.

nodes.name: Higgs Field
nodes.definition: Scalar field with nonzero vacuum expectation value in the Standard Model; its interactions participate in electroweak symmetry breaking and mass generation.

nodes.name: Higgs Boson
nodes.definition: Observed spin-0 excitation of the Higgs field, consistent with the Standard Model scalar sector.

nodes.name: Quark
nodes.definition: Fermionic matter field carrying color and fractional electric charge; six flavors occur in three generations.

nodes.name: Lepton
nodes.definition: Fermionic matter class including charged leptons and neutrinos; leptons do not carry QCD color charge.

nodes.name: Gauge Boson
nodes.definition: Quantum excitation associated with gauge fields; photon, gluons and W/Z bosons mediate Standard Model gauge interactions.

nodes.name: Photon
nodes.definition: Massless spin-1 gauge boson of unbroken electromagnetic U(1).

nodes.name: Gluon
nodes.definition: Eight massless spin-1 gauge bosons of SU(3) color; unlike photons, gluons carry the charge of their own gauge group.

nodes.name: W Boson
nodes.definition: Massive charged weak gauge boson produced after electroweak symmetry breaking.

nodes.name: Z Boson
nodes.definition: Massive neutral weak gauge boson produced after electroweak symmetry breaking.

nodes.name: Topological Charge
nodes.definition: Integer or otherwise quantized invariant characterizing certain globally distinct field configurations; precise definition depends on the theory and boundary conditions.

nodes.name: Instanton
nodes.definition: Finite-action Euclidean gauge-field configuration associated with nontrivial topological sectors and tunneling phenomena in appropriate theories.

nodes.name: Magnetic Monopole
nodes.definition: Hypothetical or model-dependent magnetic-charge configuration; in gauge theories monopoles can arise as topological defects after symmetry breaking.

nodes.name: Vortex Defect
nodes.definition: Localized configuration characterized by nontrivial winding around a core; examples occur in condensed matter and field theories.

nodes.name: Domain Wall
nodes.definition: Interface separating regions associated with distinct vacua or order parameters; may be topologically stable when boundary conditions support it.

nodes.name: Berry Phase
nodes.definition: Geometric phase accumulated during adiabatic cyclic evolution in parameter space; depends on global structure of eigenstates over the parameter manifold.

nodes.name: Chern Number
nodes.definition: Integer characteristic invariant built from curvature of a bundle; appears in quantized Hall response and topological band theory.

nodes.name: Quantum Anomaly
nodes.definition: Classical symmetry that fails after quantization; gauge anomalies can obstruct consistency and must cancel in a consistent chiral gauge theory.

nodes.name: Index Theorem
nodes.definition: Relates analytical data such as zero modes of differential operators to topological invariants; links Dirac operators, gauge backgrounds and anomaly calculations.

nodes.name: Dirac Operator
nodes.definition: First-order differential operator acting on spinor fields; its index and spectrum connect geometry, topology and quantum field theory.

nodes.name: Braid Group
nodes.definition: Group describing equivalence classes of braidings of strands; replaces simple permutation structure in two-dimensional exchange problems.

nodes.name: Anyon
nodes.definition: Two-dimensional quasiparticle whose exchange can realize statistics more general than bosonic or fermionic permutation, often described through braid representations.

nodes.name: Topological Order
nodes.definition: Long-range quantum organization characterized by features such as robust degeneracy, anyonic excitations and nonlocal order parameters rather than conventional symmetry breaking alone.

nodes.name: Quantum Information
nodes.definition: Framework treating quantum states, channels, entanglement, measurement and computation as information-bearing structures.

nodes.name: Entanglement
nodes.definition: Nonseparable structure of a composite quantum state; correlations cannot generally be reproduced by assigning independent states to subsystems.

nodes.name: Symmetry Breaking
nodes.definition: Situation in which equations or underlying theory possess a symmetry while a chosen state or vacuum does not preserve the full symmetry.

nodes.name: Vacuum Manifold
nodes.definition: Set of degenerate minima of a potential or effective energy; its topology can determine possible defects.

nodes.name: Order Parameter
nodes.definition: Observable or field distinguishing phases or symmetry-breaking patterns; its target space can possess nontrivial topology.

nodes.name: Trajectory–Topology Bridge
nodes.definition: Project-level grammar relating state, transition, path, connectivity, boundary, defect and repair without identifying symbolic mythology with physics.

nodes.name: Angelic Trajectory
nodes.definition: Analytical representation of messenger narratives as authorized transmission across a boundary; not a physical trajectory.

nodes.name: Demonic Trajectory
nodes.definition: Analytical representation of adversarial narratives as obstruction, diversion, fixation or extraction; not a physical field or particle.

research_notes: The Standard Model is an experimentally successful quantum field theory for electromagnetic, weak and strong interactions, but excludes gravity and leaves major questions such as dark matter unresolved.
Spin is intrinsic angular momentum represented through symmetry; avoid the misleading picture of elementary particles as literal spinning balls.

Topology becomes physically consequential when global configuration or field structure cannot be removed by continuous deformation; gauge bundles, defects, instantons and geometric phases are major examples.
Anomalies are especially important because they show that a classical symmetry can fail after quantization; gauge anomalies threaten consistency and must cancel in the Standard Model.

The bridge to mythology is a relational vocabulary: state, boundary, transmission, obstruction, trajectory, connectivity, defect and repair. It is not a physical identification of supernatural beings.
